claim: Mendelian Disorders of the Epigenetic Machinery (MDEMs) have shared disease manifestations despite having different causative genes.
source: Although each Mendelian Disorder of the Epigenetic Machinery (MDEM) has a different causative gene, there are shared disease manifestations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Phenotypic convergence in MDEMs is hypothesized to be a consequence of shared epigenetic alterations.
source: We hypothesize that this phenotypic convergence is a consequence of shared epigenetic alterations.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: 587 loci show shared disruption across all three MDEMs studied (KS1, KS2, and RT1).
source: identify 587 loci and 264 genes with shared disruption across all three MDEMs
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract with specific numbers.

claim: 264 genes show shared disruption across all three MDEMs studied (KS1, KS2, and RT1).
source: identify 587 loci and 264 genes with shared disruption across all three MDEMs
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract with specific numbers.

claim: Disruption of chromatin accessibility at promoters often disrupts downstream gene expression.
source: We show that disruption of chromatin accessibility at promoters often disrupts downstream gene expression
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Subtle expression alterations of multiple IgA-relevant genes collectively contribute to IgA deficiency in KS1.
source: Subtle expression alterations of multiple, IgA-relevant genes, collectively contribute to IgA deficiency in KS1 and RT1, but not in KS2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gene set analysis and IgA measurements in Figure 5.

claim: Subtle expression alterations of multiple IgA-relevant genes collectively contribute to IgA deficiency in RT1.
source: Subtle expression alterations of multiple, IgA-relevant genes, collectively contribute to IgA deficiency in KS1 and RT1, but not in KS2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gene set analysis in Figure 5.

claim: IgA deficiency does not occur in KS2 despite occurring in KS1 and RT1.
source: Subtle expression alterations of multiple, IgA-relevant genes, collectively contribute to IgA deficiency in KS1 and RT1, but not in KS2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by IgA measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MDEMs are caused by coding variants disrupting genes encoding for epigenetic regulators.
source: MDEMs are caused by coding variants disrupting genes encoding for epigenetic regulators, which are generally very intolerant to loss-of-function variation (Boukas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Epigenetic regulators are generally very intolerant to loss-of-function variation.
source: MDEMs are caused by coding variants disrupting genes encoding for epigenetic regulators, which are generally very intolerant to loss-of-function variation (Boukas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boukas et al., 2019.

claim: MDEM pathogenesis follows a causal chain: coding variant disrupts epigenetic regulator → downstream epigenomic abnormalities → transcriptome perturbations → phenotype.
source: This implies the following causal chain underlying MDEM pathogenesis: a coding variant disrupts an epigenetic regulator, leading to downstream epigenomic abnormalities, which in turn give rise to the phenotype, likely by perturbing the transcriptome (Figure 1A).
evidence: This causal chain is explicitly described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Kabuki syndrome type 1 (KS1) is caused by haploinsufficiency in histone methyltransferase KMT2D.
source: Kabuki syndrome types 1 and 2 [KS1 and KS2], caused by haploinsufficiency in histone methyltransferases KMT2D and KDM6A, respectively
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Kabuki syndrome type 2 (KS2) is caused by haploinsufficiency in histone methyltransferase KDM6A.
source: Kabuki syndrome types 1 and 2 [KS1 and KS2], caused by haploinsufficiency in histone methyltransferases KMT2D and KDM6A, respectively
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome type 1 (RT1) is caused by haploinsufficiency in histone acetyltransferase CREBBP.
source: Rubinstein-Taybi type 1 [RT1], caused by haploinsufficiency in histone acetyltransferase CREBBP
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: KS1 and KS2 were clinically indistinguishable prior to the discovery of the underlying genes.
source: two that were clinically indistinguishable prior to the discovery of the underlying genes (Kabuki syndrome types 1 and 2 [KS1 and KS2], caused by haploinsufficiency in histone methyltransferases KMT2D and KDM6A, respectively)
evidence: This is stated as historical fact in the introduction.

claim: Shared phenotypes of KS1, KS2, and RT1 include intellectual disability, growth retardation, and immune dysfunction.
source: The shared phenotypes of these three syndromes include intellectual disability, growth retardation, and immune dysfunction
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In KS1, immune dysfunction includes hypogammaglobulinemia with low IgA as a consistent feature.
source: In KS1, the immune dysfunction includes hypogammaglobulinemia with low IgA as a consistent feature, as well as abnormal cell maturation which has mostly been characterized in B cells (Margot et al., 2020; Lindsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: In KS1, immune dysfunction includes abnormal cell maturation which has mostly been characterized in B cells.
source: In KS1, the immune dysfunction includes hypogammaglobulinemia with low IgA as a consistent feature, as well as abnormal cell maturation which has mostly been characterized in B cells (Margot et al., 2020; Lindsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: RT1 can manifest with hypogammaglobulinemia and reduction of mature B cells.
source: RT1 can also manifest with hypogammaglobulinemia and reduction of mature B cells (Saettini et al., 2020.)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The immune defects in KS1 and RT1 are thought to at least partly explain the increased susceptibility to infections.
source: These defects in KS1 and RT1 are thought to (at least partly) explain the increased susceptibility to infections.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the literature.

claim: In KS2, there is some evidence of increased infection susceptibility and hypogammaglobulinemia.
source: In KS2, the immune phenotype has been less extensively studied, in part due to the rarity of the disorder, but there is some evidence of increased infection susceptibility and hypogammaglobulinemia (Margot et al., 2020; Frans et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The IgA deficiency in KS1 mice closely resembles what is seen in patients with Kabuki syndrome.
source: In mice, the immune phenotypes have been studied in depth only in KS1, where the IgA deficiency closely resembles what is seen in patients with Kabuki syndrome.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding from previous mouse studies.

claim: 3938 ATAC peaks are differentially accessible at the 10% FDR level in KS1 vs. wild-type mice.
source: Starting with a differential accessibility analysis of 7 KS1 vs. 12 wild-type mice (Materials and methods), we discovered 3938 ATAC peaks differentially accessible at the 10% FDR level.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the differential accessibility analysis.

claim: 1062 (27%) of the differentially accessible peaks in KS1 overlap promoters.
source: Of these, 1062 (27%) overlapped promoters (defined as ±2 kb from the TSS), and 2876 (73%) were in distal regulatory elements (defined as ATAC peaks outside of promoters).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of differential peaks.

claim: 2876 (73%) of the differentially accessible peaks in KS1 are in distal regulatory elements.
source: Of these, 1062 (27%) overlapped promoters (defined as ±2 kb from the TSS), and 2876 (73%) were in distal regulatory elements (defined as ATAC peaks outside of promoters).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of differential peaks.

claim: 68.5% of promoter peaks differentially accessible in KS1 are also differential in KS2.
source: We found that 68.5% of promoter peaks differentially accessible in KS1 are also differential in KS2 (Figure 2A; p < 2.2e-16, 5 KS2 vs. 12 wild-type mice)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the overlap analysis with statistical significance.

claim: 733 promoter peaks are identified as shared differentially accessible between KS1 and KS2 at the 10% FDR level.
source: at the 10% FDR level, we identified 733 such peaks.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis.

claim: For 724 of the 733 (98.8%) shared promoter peaks between KS1 and KS2, accessibility is altered in the same direction in the two syndromes.
source: For 724 of the 733 (98.8%), accessibility is altered in the same direction in the two syndromes (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing concordance of effect directions.

claim: Approximately 67% of promoter peaks disrupted in both KS1 and KS2 are differential in RT1 as well.
source: Out of these 724 promoter peaks disrupted in both KS1 and KS2, we discovered that approximately 67% are differential in RT1 as well (Figure 2C; p < 2.2e-16, 5 RT1 vs. 7 wild-type mice)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the three-way overlap analysis with statistical significance.

claim: 420 promoter peaks show disruption in all three disorders (KS1, KS2, RT1) at the 10% FDR level with concordant effect sizes.
source: In total, we identified 420 promoter peaks that show disruption in all three disorders at the 10% FDR level with concordant effect sizes (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding from the three-way overlap analysis.

claim: The new overlap analysis approach provides >4 times more shared peaks than the standard approach of computing intersections of differential hits.
source: This is >4 times more shared peaks than we find if we perform separate differential analyses and compute the intersection of the resulting differential hits (100 peaks), highlighting that our new approach provides substantial gain in empirical power, as suggested by our simulations.
evidence: This is a comparison of methods showing improved performance.

claim: KS1 mice cluster close to RT1 in PCA based on shared disrupted promoter peaks.
source: The KS1 mice cluster close to RT1, while KS1 and KS2 cluster separately from each other, with KS2 being closer than KS1 to wild-type, indicating smaller effect sizes of the accessibility alterations.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: KS2 clusters closer to wild-type than KS1, indicating smaller effect sizes of the accessibility alterations in KS2.
source: The KS1 mice cluster close to RT1, while KS1 and KS2 cluster separately from each other, with KS2 being closer than KS1 to wild-type, indicating smaller effect sizes of the accessibility alterations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: KS2 female mice are expected to be mosaic with respect to Kdm6a knockout because Kdm6a is on the X chromosome.
source: However, it should be noted here that, since Kdm6a is on the X chromosome, the KS2 female mice are expected to be mosaic with respect to Kdm6a knockout, and this may explain the smaller magnitude of their accessibility defects.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the observed smaller effect sizes in KS2.

claim: 50.8% of distal regulatory elements differential in KS1 are estimated as differential in KS2.
source: Specifically, 50.8% of elements differential in KS1 were estimated as differential in KS2 (p < 2.2e-16)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the overlap analysis of distal elements.

claim: 815 distal regulatory elements are confidently labeled as shared between KS1 and KS2 at the 10% FDR level.
source: with 815 confidently labeled such elements (10% FDR).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis.

claim: 806 out of 815 (98.9%) shared distal regulatory elements between KS1 and KS2 show agreement in directionality.
source: As with promoters, we observed agreement in directionality for the vast majority of peaks (806 out of the 815; Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing concordance of effect directions.

claim: 35.6% of KS1/2 shared distal regulatory elements with concordant directionality are differential in RT1.
source: Of the KS1/2 shared elements with concordant directionality, 35.6% are differential in RT1 (p = 0.0025)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the three-way overlap analysis with statistical significance.

claim: 167 distal regulatory elements show shared disruption across all three MDEMs at the 10% FDR level.
source: yielding a total of 167 shared disrupted distal regulatory elements across the three MDEMs (10% FDR; Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding from the three-way overlap analysis.

claim: Shared hits show a 7.1-fold enrichment at promoters compared to distal elements.
source: We note that, collectively, the shared hits show a 7.1-fold enrichment at promoters compared to distal elements (Fisher's test, p < 2.2e-16).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing the distribution of shared hits.

claim: KS1 and KS2 share a greater proportion of their abnormalities than either KS1 or KS2 compared to RT1.
source: Finally, comparing the three MDEMs in a pairwise fashion, we observed that KS1 and KS2 share a greater proportion of their abnormalities than either KS1 or KS2 compared to RT1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a comparative finding from pairwise overlap analyses.

claim: 83.5% of significantly disrupted promoter peaks in KS1 mutants show increased accessibility.
source: We found that, at promoters, both the KS1 and KS2 mutants exhibit a substantial shift toward increased accessibility (83.5% and 91.2%, respectively, of significantly disrupted promoter peaks; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the directionality analysis.

claim: 91.2% of significantly disrupted promoter peaks in KS2 mutants show increased accessibility.
source: We found that, at promoters, both the KS1 and KS2 mutants exhibit a substantial shift toward increased accessibility (83.5% and 91.2%, respectively, of significantly disrupted promoter peaks; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the directionality analysis.

claim: 62.2% of differentially accessible promoter peaks in RT1 mutants show decreased accessibility.
source: even though in the RT1 mutants the majority (62.2%) of differentially accessible promoter peaks show the opposite pattern, with a shift toward decreased accessibility (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the directionality analysis.

claim: 41.6% of disrupted distal regulatory elements in KS1 show increased accessibility.
source: In contrast to promoters, disrupted distal regulatory elements in all cases are more evenly split: the percentage with increased accessibility is 41.6% in KS1, 39.3% in KS2, and 60% in RT1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the directionality analysis.

claim: 39.3% of disrupted distal regulatory elements in KS2 show increased accessibility.
source: In contrast to promoters, disrupted distal regulatory elements in all cases are more evenly split: the percentage with increased accessibility is 41.6% in KS1, 39.3% in KS2, and 60% in RT1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the directionality analysis.

claim: 60% of disrupted distal regulatory elements in RT1 show increased accessibility.
source: In contrast to promoters, disrupted distal regulatory elements in all cases are more evenly split: the percentage with increased accessibility is 41.6% in KS1, 39.3% in KS2, and 60% in RT1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the directionality analysis.

claim: When considering the top 1000 promoter peaks, 45.4% of genes downstream show differential expression in KS1.
source: When considering the top 1000 promoter peaks, the percentage of differentially expressed downstream genes is 45.4% in KS1, 42% in KS2, and 40% in RT1 (Materials and methods; Figure 3—source data 1 contains such genes detected at the 10% FDR level).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the integrated chromatin-expression analysis.

claim: When considering the top 1000 promoter peaks, 42% of genes downstream show differential expression in KS2.
source: When considering the top 1000 promoter peaks, the percentage of differentially expressed downstream genes is 45.4% in KS1, 42% in KS2, and 40% in RT1 (Materials and methods; Figure 3—source data 1 contains such genes detected at the 10% FDR level).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the integrated chromatin-expression analysis.

claim: When considering the top 1000 promoter peaks, 40% of genes downstream show differential expression in RT1.
source: When considering the top 1000 promoter peaks, the percentage of differentially expressed downstream genes is 45.4% in KS1, 42% in KS2, and 40% in RT1 (Materials and methods; Figure 3—source data 1 contains such genes detected at the 10% FDR level).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the integrated chromatin-expression analysis.

claim: The percentage of differentially expressed genes downstream of differentially accessible promoters drops substantially as the cutoff for labeling a promoter as differentially accessible becomes less stringent.
source: In all three syndromes, this percentage gradually drops substantially as the cutoff for labeling a promoter as differentially accessible becomes less stringent (Figure 3A), indicating a clear relationship between abnormal promoter accessibility and downstream gene expression dysregulation (with the relationship being noisier in RT1).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is strong concordance between the direction of abnormal changes at disrupted promoter-gene pairs: increased or decreased promoter accessibility correlates with increased or decreased gene expression, respectively.
source: Emphasizing this relationship, we discovered strong concordance between the direction of abnormal changes at the disrupted promoter-gene pairs: increased or decreased promoter accessibility correlates with increased or decreased gene expression, respectively (Figure 3B, C and D; Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC = 0.78 for KS1, 0.84 for KS2, and 0.82 for RT1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with correlation coefficients provided.

claim: The Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC is 0.78 for KS1.
source: Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC = 0.78 for KS1, 0.84 for KS2, and 0.82 for RT1
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: The Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC is 0.84 for KS2.
source: Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC = 0.78 for KS1, 0.84 for KS2, and 0.82 for RT1
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: The Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC is 0.82 for RT1.
source: Pearson correlation between promoter accessibility logFC and gene expression logFC = 0.78 for KS1, 0.84 for KS2, and 0.82 for RT1
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: Genes downstream of shared disrupted promoter peaks have a higher chance of dysregulated expression compared to genes downstream of disorder-specific disrupted peaks.
source: We invariably found the genes downstream of the shared disrupted peaks to have a higher chance of dysregulated expression (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting our hypothesis that the chromatin alterations at these peaks are more likely to have functional impact.
evidence: This is a comparative finding supporting the functional relevance of shared hits.

claim: 397 differentially expressed genes are shared between KS1 and KS2 with concordant direction of effect at 10% FDR.
source: Specifically, we found 397 differentially expressed genes shared between them with concordant direction of effect (10% FDR; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the overlap analysis of gene expression.

claim: 78.8% of genes differentially expressed in both KS1 and KS2 are estimated to be differential in RT1.
source: We then estimated 78.8% of these to be differential in RT1 (Figure 4)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the three-way overlap analysis.

claim: 264 genes are shared differentially expressed across all three disorders (KS1, KS2, RT1) at 10% FDR.
source: resulting in 264 genes shared across the three disorders (10% FDR)
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding from the three-way overlap analysis.

claim: Among the 264 shared differentially expressed genes, there is a preponderance of downregulated genes (175 downregulated vs. 89 upregulated).
source: with a preponderance of downregulated genes (Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—source data 2; 175 downregulated vs. 89 upregulated genes).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the directionality of shared expression changes.

claim: The 264 shared differentially expressed genes are significantly enriched in the set of genes with shared disruption of promoter accessibility (p = 0.0001).
source: While these 264 genes are significantly enriched in the set of genes with shared disruption of promoter accessibility (p = 0.0001), the magnitude of this enrichment is modest (29 genes in the intersection; odds ratio = 2.37, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from enrichment analysis.

claim: 29 genes show both shared differential expression and shared differential promoter accessibility across all three MDEMs.
source: the magnitude of this enrichment is modest (29 genes in the intersection; odds ratio = 2.37, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the intersection analysis.

claim: The odds ratio for enrichment of shared differentially expressed genes in the set of genes with shared disrupted promoters is 2.37.
source: the magnitude of this enrichment is modest (29 genes in the intersection; odds ratio = 2.37, Table 1).
evidence: This is a specific statistical measure from enrichment analysis.

claim: 99 genes show shared differential expression and harbor shared disrupted regulatory elements nearby (±1 Mb from their promoter peaks).
source: The number of genes in the intersection increases to 99 when we also include those harboring shared disrupted regulatory elements nearby (±1 Mb from their promoter peaks).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding when expanding the definition to include distal elements.

claim: There is convergent dysregulation of gene expression in the three MDEMs which is not always a direct downstream consequence of shared epigenetic alterations.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that there is convergent dysregulation of gene expression in these three MDEMs, which is not always a direct downstream consequence of the shared epigenetic alterations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings regarding the relationship between chromatin and expression changes.

claim: In KS1 and KS2, but not in RT1, the top differentially expressed genes are more likely to have disrupted promoters than genes further down the differential list.
source: Nevertheless, in KS1 and KS2 – but not in RT1 – the top differentially expressed genes are more likely to have disrupted promoters than genes further down the differential list (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Transcription factors of the NF-kB pathway appear affected at the expression level in all three disorders.
source: Notable among the significant hits (Figure 4—source data 3) are motifs recognized by transcription factors of the NF-kB pathway, which appears affected at the expression level in the three disorders.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The regulatory network disruption in the three MDEMs does not converge to a few dominant transcription factors.
source: Overall, this analysis indicates that the regulatory network disruption in the three MDEMs does not converge to a few dominant transcription factors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the motif enrichment analysis results.

claim: Transcription factors expressed in CD19+ B cells show global dysregulation in KS1 (p = 0.001).
source: We then examined the ranks of these transcription factors in the KS1 p-value distribution and observed a strong shift indicative of global dysregulation (Figure 5A; p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from gene set analysis.

claim: Genes known to lead to IgA deficiency when individually knocked out in mouse show a collective shift toward lower p-values in KS1 (p = 0.03).
source: Examination of the KS1 p-value ranks of these genes also highlighted a collective shift toward lower p-values (Figure 5B; p = 0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from gene set analysis.

claim: The collective dysregulation of IgA deficiency genes is observed in RT1.
source: Turning our attention to KS2 and RT1, we observed similar results for transcription factors, with substantial contribution from a set of transcription factors dysregulated in all three MDEMs (Figure 5A, C). However, when assessing the IgA deficiency genes, we only observed the signal in RT1, and not in KS2 (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene set analysis comparing the three disorders.

claim: The collective dysregulation of IgA deficiency genes is not observed in KS2.
source: However, when assessing the IgA deficiency genes, we only observed the signal in RT1, and not in KS2 (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene set analysis comparing the three disorders.

claim: There is no difference in serum IgA levels between KS2 and wild-type mice (p = 0.8).
source: In agreement with the collective behavior of IgA-related genes, we found no difference in IgA levels between the KS2 and wild-type, while we recapitulated our previous result of IgA deficiency in KS1 mice (Pilarowski et al., 2020; Figure 5E; p = 0.8 for KS2 vs. WT, p = 0.0008 for KS1 vs. WT, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from IgA measurements with statistical testing.

claim: KS1 mice show IgA deficiency compared to wild-type (p = 0.0008).
source: In agreement with the collective behavior of IgA-related genes, we found no difference in IgA levels between the KS2 and wild-type, while we recapitulated our previous result of IgA deficiency in KS1 mice (Pilarowski et al., 2020; Figure 5E; p = 0.8 for KS2 vs. WT, p = 0.0008 for KS1 vs. WT, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from IgA measurements with statistical testing, replicating a previous result.

claim: There is no evidence that collective defects in expression of transcription factors are driven by similar shifts toward abnormal promoter accessibility, except for transcription factor promoters in RT1 (p = 0.04).
source: Finally, we found no evidence that these collective defects in the expression of transcription factors and IgA deficiency associated genes are driven by similar shifts toward abnormal promoter accessibility, with the exception of transcription factor promoters in RT1 (p = 0.04).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of promoter accessibility for specific gene sets.

claim: The three MDEMs studied have shared alterations at the chromatin and gene expression level in B cells.
source: We have taken a first step toward validating this hypothesis, by showing that three MDEMs caused by loss-of-function variants in three distinct epigenetic regulators have shared alterations at the chromatin and gene expression level in B cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the Discussion.

claim: Many chromatin changes at promoters are linked to downstream gene expression changes.
source: Nonetheless, our results provide some evidence of functionality, as illustrated by the fact that: (a) many chromatin changes at promoters are linked to downstream gene expression changes
evidence: This is stated as evidence for functionality in the Discussion, summarizing findings from Figure 3.

claim: Systematic expression changes affect genes known to contribute to specific, well-characterized phenotypic features (IgA deficiency, abnormal B-cell maturation) of MDEMs.
source: and (b) systematic expression changes affect genes known to contribute to specific, well-characterized phenotypic features (IgA deficiency, abnormal B-cell maturation) of these MDEMs.
evidence: This is stated as evidence for functionality in the Discussion, summarizing findings from Figure 5.

claim: IgA deficiency has been observed in both male and female KS1 patients.
source: While it is known that sex differences can influence immune responses and deficiencies (Klein and Flanagan, 2016), IgA deficiency has been observed in both male and female KS1 patients, and characterized in both male and female KS1 mice (Pilarowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations in the Discussion.

claim: IgA deficiency has been characterized in both male and female KS1 mice.
source: While it is known that sex differences can influence immune responses and deficiencies (Klein and Flanagan, 2016), IgA deficiency has been observed in both male and female KS1 patients, and characterized in both male and female KS1 mice (Pilarowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation in the Discussion.

claim: The immune dysfunction in KS1 mice has been shown to mimic many aspects of what is seen in patients.
source: However, the immune dysfunction in KS1 mice has previously been shown to mimic many aspects of what is seen in patients (Pilarowski et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation in the Discussion.

claim: The findings point toward a generalized, systems-level dysregulation in MDEMs, with a multitude of cellular processes/pathways affected.
source: In terms of understanding the pathogenesis of MDEMs, our findings clearly point toward a generalized, systems-level dysregulation, with a multitude of cellular processes/pathways affected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings in the Discussion.

claim: There is greater molecular overlap between KS1 and KS2 than between either of them and RT1.
source: It is notable that we find greater molecular overlap between KS1 and KS2 than between either of them and RT1, in agreement with the greater similarity between the two KS types at the phenotypic level.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the overlap analyses discussed in the Results section.

claim: Abnormalities in IgA deficiency genes are present in KS1 and RT1 but absent in KS2.
source: It should be mentioned, however, that specific sub-phenotypes provide exceptions to this rule, as evidenced by the abnormalities in IgA deficiency genes, which are present in KS1 and RT1 but are absent in KS2.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 5 discussed in the Discussion.

claim: Almost all of the shared disrupted peaks at promoters exhibit a shift toward a more open chromatin state.
source: One unexpected finding was that, at promoters, almost all of the shared disrupted peaks exhibit a shift toward a more open chromatin state
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 2F discussed in the Discussion.

claim: The causative mutations of all three disorders would theoretically be expected to push toward a more closed chromatin state, based on the specific histone marks they are thought to affect.
source: even though the causative mutations of all three disorders would theoretically be expected to push toward a more closed chromatin state, based on the specific histone marks they are thought to affect (Fahrner and Bjornsson, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation in the Discussion.

claim: Many of the shared genes uncovered in this study are not known to be directly targeted by the KMT2D, KDM6A, or CREBBP proteins.
source: Finally, there is the possibility that the causative mutations lead to a non-specific cellular compensatory response, which causes increased chromatin openness at several genomic locations such as the adaptive stress response (Brose et al., 2012). The latter is supported by the fact that many of the shared genes uncovered in this study are not known to be directly targeted by the KMT2D, KDM6A, or CREBBP proteins.
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence for a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: The study differs from recent studies of DNA methylation in the peripheral blood of MDEM patients that derive 'episignatures' for phenotypic prediction.
source: We note that our study differs from recent studies of DNA methylation in the peripheral blood of MDEM patients (Aref-Eshghi et al., 2020; Sobreira et al., 2017; Butcher et al., 2017). In these studies, the goal is to derive 'episignatures' with the capacity for robust phenotypic prediction.
evidence: This is a comparison to other studies with citations in the Discussion.

claim: The strategy in this study is specifically designed to yield a catalog of abnormalities with primary functional role in shared MDEM pathogenesis.
source: our strategy is specifically designed to yield a catalog of abnormalities with primary functional role in shared MDEM pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's design goal in the Discussion.

claim: MDEMs are effectively complex disorders with respect to their molecular pathogenesis, arising from widely distributed epigenetic perturbations across the genome.
source: Finally, we suggest that MDEMs are effectively complex disorders with respect to their molecular pathogenesis, arising from widely distributed epigenetic perturbations across the genome.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretation stated in the Discussion.

claim: The study used only female mice to enable comparison between all three disease models.
source: We performed all experiments in female mice to enable a comparison between all three disease models, as Kdm6a (KS2 model) is present on the X chromosome, and its full knockout is in our experience uniformly lethal in male mice.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice in the Sex disaggregation section.

claim: Complete loss (full knockout) of Kdm6a is lethal in male mice.
source: as Kdm6a is on the X chromosome (KS2 mouse model), and its complete loss (full knockout) is lethal in male mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experience.

claim: The new overlap analysis method provides substantially greater ability to estimate the size of the overlap compared to the standard approach.
source: Our results confirmed that our method provides substantially greater ability to estimate the size of the overlap (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation study described in Materials and methods.

claim: The new overlap analysis method had an average proportion of false discoveries equal to 10.9%, close to the nominal FDR of 10%.
source: In addition, our method had an average proportion of false discoveries (i.e. features labeled as belonging to the overlap that were not truly differential across the experiments) equal to 10.9%, very close to the nominal FDR of 10%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation study validating the method.

claim: 99.88% of the 78,193 genomic intervals identified as ATAC peaks overlapped DNase Hypersensitivity Sites in B cells from the ENCODE project.
